title: Wonder Bets Big on Indian Food With Dabba, Its First Desi Chain Concept
excerpt: The $2-billion food-hall startup is testing an Indian restaurant brand in Philadelphia, joining a wave of ventures racing to make butter chicken as ubiquitous as pad thai.
body:
Marc Lore's Wonder, the food-hall and delivery venture backed by over $2 billion in private funding, has quietly launched its most culturally ambitious concept yet: an Indian restaurant brand called Dabba.

## What Is Dabba?

Named after Mumbai's legendary dabbawallas — the thousands of lunch delivery workers who have been ferrying home-cooked meals across the city for over 130 years — Dabba is currently testing in four Philadelphia-area Wonder locations. The menu features Indian staples including samosas ($8.95), chicken tikka masala, butter chicken ($19.95), and lamb vindaloo, all developed by Wonder's in-house culinary team with chefs experienced in Indian cuisine.

If the test succeeds, Dabba will roll out across Wonder's more than 100 storefronts on the East Coast, making it one of the few US chains offering Indian food at scale. The company, which also owns Grubhub and Blue Apron, plans to enter Texas next year and is eyeing an IPO by 2028.

## The Scaling Challenge

Indian cuisine's complexity is both its magic and its barrier to chain-scale expansion. The layering of spices, the slow-cooked bases, the regional variation — these are not easily standardised across a hundred kitchens. Wonder believes its vertically integrated model, where curries and sauces are developed in-house, produced centrally, and finished to order at individual locations, can solve this.

"We've built a model that allows us to control the full process — from recipe development through production and final preparation," a Wonder spokesperson said. The four-store test will allow the company to refine recipes before scaling.

The largest existing Indian chains in America remain relatively small: Bawarchi Indian Cuisine with 50 units, Honest Restaurants with 42, and Curry Up Now with 19. The UK's cult favourite Dishoom is also planning its first American outpost in New York, backed by private-equity firm L Catterton.

## A Tipping Point for Indian Cuisine

Dabba arrives at a moment when Indian food's trajectory in the US feels genuinely different. Industry forecasters have named Indian cuisine among the top menu trends for 2026, with Keralan flavours and regional specialities gaining particular attention. Gen Z and millennial diners show increasing preference for Indian fare, and fast-casual Indian concepts like Tarka and Biju's are expanding in multiple markets.

At the high end, Michelin-starred Indian restaurants — Indienne in Chicago, Semma in New York, Rania in Washington — are rewriting perceptions of what Indian dining can be. At the retail level, premium brands like Gymkhana Fine Foods are landing on Whole Foods shelves nationwide.

## The Diaspora Angle

For Indian Americans, the mainstreaming of desi food is both gratifying and complicated. There is pride in seeing butter chicken and samosas offered alongside sushi and Thai noodles at a platform as large as Wonder. There is also the familiar worry about flattening — the reduction of India's staggeringly diverse food traditions into a handful of North Indian greatest hits.

Dabba's name, at least, suggests an awareness of the culture it is drawing from. Whether the food can honour that culture while hitting Wonder's consistency targets is the test that matters.

## What's Next

Dabba is available now at four Wonder locations in the Philadelphia area. A systemwide rollout will depend on the test's performance, but Wonder's scale and ambition suggest Indian food is about to get a platform it has never had in American chain dining. Whether that is a breakthrough or a compromise depends on what ends up in the dabba.

*Sources: Restaurant Business Online, CNBC, Nation's Restaurant News*
